# Our model vs CGM-style trend alarms (real patients)

**Research prototype. Not a medical device, not for clinical use.** Generated by
`python -m src.eval.trend_comparison --data-dir data/external/shanghai` (ShanghaiT2DM, CC BY 4.0, not redistributed).

CGM makers already sell predictive low alerts that extrapolate the recent trend (Dexcom G7 "Urgent Low Soon",
Medtronic's "alert before low"). This page asks what a learned model adds over that idea, on 100 real patients (109 recording periods, 389 low episodes).

## Result

**At the same number of alerts (about 1.0 a day), our model's alerts were followed by a real low more often (39% vs 36% for a 20-minute trend alarm) and warned of 54% of lows at least 30 minutes ahead (vs 48%), with a median warning of 35 min. The edge is real but modest: a well-tuned trend alarm is just as good at 15 minutes.**

| Alarm | Warned >= 15 min | Warned >= 30 min | Median lead (min) | Alerts / patient-day | PPV per alert |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| A. Our model, checked every 30 min (deployed) | 53% | 35% (28%-40%) | 25 | 0.61 (0.46-0.78) | 44% (38%-50%) |
| B. Our model, checked every 5 min | 84% | 54% (48%-60%) | 35 | 0.98 (0.77-1.24) | 39% (34%-44%) |
| C. Trend alarm: projected to reach 70 within 20 min (the Dexcom idea) | 75% | 40% (36%-44%) | 25 | 0.82 (0.65-1.00) | 42% (36%-48%) |
| C. Trend alarm: projected to reach 70 within 60 min (the Medtronic idea) | 90% | 79% (75%-83%) | 60 | 2.65 (2.34-2.98) | 15% (11%-18%) |
| D. Trend alarm, 20-min projection, level 72 mg/dL (matched alerts/day) | 85% | 48% (43%-53%) | 25 | 0.99 (0.79-1.20) | 36% (30%-41%) |
| D. Trend alarm, 30-min projection, level 67 mg/dL (matched alerts/day) | 76% | 49% (45%-53%) | 30 | 0.98 (0.80-1.18) | 34% (28%-40%) |
| D. Trend alarm, 60-min projection, level 45 mg/dL (matched alerts/day) | 55% | 43% (36%-49%) | 40 | 0.98 (0.83-1.12) | 24% (18%-30%) |

95% CIs resample recording periods.

## Paired differences: our model (B) minus each matched trend alarm (D)

Percentage points, 1000 paired resamples of recording periods. *P* = share of resamples where our model is better.

| Trend alarm | Warned >= 15 min | Warned >= 30 min | PPV | Alerts / day | P (>= 30 min) | P (PPV) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 20-min projection, level 72 mg/dL | -1.3 (-5.2 to +2.4) | +5.9 (-0.5 to +12.4) | +3.3 (+0.4 to +5.8) | -0.01 (-0.08 to +0.07) | 0.95 | 0.98 |
| 30-min projection, level 67 mg/dL | +8.2 (+2.7 to +13.4) | +4.9 (-1.3 to +10.4) | +4.9 (+2.0 to +7.4) | +0.00 (-0.07 to +0.10) | 0.93 | 1.00 |
| 60-min projection, level 45 mg/dL | +28.8 (+21.0 to +36.8) | +10.5 (+2.1 to +17.4) | +15.1 (+11.6 to +18.4) | +0.00 (-0.14 to +0.16) | 0.99 | 1.00 |

## Reading this honestly

* **The prediction adds a real but modest gain over a tuned trend alarm.** More of its alerts are real and the
  warning comes earlier; at 15 minutes ahead a simple trend alarm is as good. The value of the product therefore
  rests as much on the reasons, the record context and the clinician view as on the forecast itself.
* **Checking every 5 minutes matters.** The same model checked every 5 minutes instead of every 30 warns of 54% instead of 35% of lows at least 30 minutes ahead (84% vs 53% at 15 min), at 0.98 instead of 0.61 alerts a day. The deployed alerts should move to 5-minute checks, with the alert budget re-tuned with clinicians.
* **A long-horizon trend alarm buys early warnings with many false alarms.** Projecting 60 minutes ahead catches
  most lows early but needs far more alerts, most of them false.

## Caveats

* The trend alarms' level was tuned on the test data itself (row D); our thresholds were set on held-out training
  patients. This favours the trend alarms.
* The real Dexcom and Medtronic algorithms are not public; rows C and D implement the trend idea at our
  episode threshold (70 mg/dL; Dexcom's alert targets 55).
* 100 patients from one Chinese centre, partly hospitalised; 15-min CGM interpolated to 5 min, which smooths
  the trend. Not Indian outpatients.
* The 30-minute warning difference against the best trend alarm is not yet statistically clear; a larger
  cohort is needed.
